summary: Used this turn for a judgment-relevant sharpening of the event-backpressure account instead of a close-out. Two new pieces, one from retained evidence and one from source. Retained timescale: the receipt bbff5b4cad8f47129ee5997bb6eee815 finished all four cases — including the default-capacity case that reaches 1129 decided entries before two nodes park — in 21.69s of test time (check.json 06:54:37→06:55:05 UTC) under ordinary paced traffic (one write per millisecond from one origin, error-free in-process delivery), so at the shipped default an unconsumed event stream parks nodes and stops progress within seconds-to-tens-of-seconds of normal operation; that is a bound from one schedule, recorded as such, not a rate claim. Drain obligation: the snapshot documents nothing that requires reading the event stream — event_capacity is described only as 'Bounded capacity for the event channel', subscribe_events only offers clones and suggests a broadcasting task for fan-out, and the handle holds a receiver from spawn_actor whether or not the application ever subscribes — while the decided-subscriber path states the opposite policy explicitly ('slow subscribers apply backpressure by causing the actor to defer pushes rather than blocking the actor loop'). The account now carries that documented contrast plus the timescale datum, with the limits updated accordingly (client-side trigger resting on the handle contract rather than a documented promise; dropped receiver unblocks; parked-set size schedule-dependent; 21.69s is a bound not a measurement; the superseded transport-jam run kept as an excluded cause). Standing position unchanged for the other two findings: the core's missing accept-phase repair for a lost Accepted (receipt 092538c6, 2-node scope recorded as a limit) and append_notify's false Ok for an unadopted index with the measured adopted-vs-unadopted boundary (receipt 78c53df3).
